extracted.intended_audience: law students, legal researchers, and attorneys researching Texas agency rules and rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Locate, identify, and interpret Texas state agency rules (final and non-final), using primary sources such as the Texas Administrative Code, the Texas Register, agency websites, and archival resources. Understand types of rule publications and procedural features (comment periods, emergency rules, citations to statutory authority) relevant to rule history and intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Texas Administrative Code (TAC) — use for final rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The Texas Administrative Code (TAC) is the official compilation of Texas agency rules and regulations; it includes all rules adopted by Texas state agencies and is published annually by the Texas Secretary of State.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The full text of the current TAC is located at the Texas Secretary of State's website. From this website, one may browse the code by title, part, chapter, subchapter, or section number, or search by keyword. The TAC does not include proposed rules, emergency rules or rules that were not adopted. The TAC is located in print in the library's collection at KFT1235 1988 .A2; the final volume of the set includes a keyword index.

rubrics_metrics.name: Texas Register — use for non-final rules and related materials
rubrics_metrics.description: The Texas Register is the official repository of all other versions of state agency rules, including proposed new rules, revised rules, and repeals of existing rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The full text of current issues is free to view and search through the Secretary of State's website. The Register is also the only source for emergency rules, comments on proposed rules, and analytical materials, unless an agency chooses to publish them on its website. In addition to rules, it includes a variety of public information (gubernatorial documents, AG opinions, public notices, corrections, etc.) and is a great source of intent information when doing a rule history. The Register was published twice weekly from 1976-1997 and is now published weekly; all back issues are archived and freely available on the University of North Texas' Portal to Texas History.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposed rules must be published multiple times
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Administrative Procedures Act, all proposed rules must be published in the Texas Register several times during the rulemaking process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every proposed rule must cite the statutory authority under which it's being promulgated; this is usually found at the beginning of the rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Every proposed rule must cite statutory authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Each proposed rule published in the Register must cite the statutory authority for its promulgation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statutory authority citation is usually found at the beginning of the rule and helps identify the enabling statute for the regulatory action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public Notice of Proposed Rulemaking — initial publication + 30-day comment
rubrics_metrics.description: The first publication of proposed rule changes or new rules is the public notice of proposed rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes a 30-day opportunity for public comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Draft Rule — republication after initial notice with additional comment time
rubrics_metrics.description: Any changes after the first public notice are republished as draft rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft rules provide additional comment time following republication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Withdrawn Rule — notice of complete withdrawal
rubrics_metrics.description: A withdrawn rule is a notice that a proposed rule has been completely withdrawn from the rulemaking process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final/Adopted Rule — adoption notice and effective date; may not reprint full text
rubrics_metrics.description: Final/adopted rule entries include a formal notice of adoption and the effective date of the rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Register often does not reprint the full text of the new rule; consult the TAC or previous Register publications to view the full rule text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emergency Rule — temporary, effective on publication, not printed in TAC
rubrics_metrics.description: Emergency rules are special, temporary rules meant to address transient emergency situations; they are not printed in the TAC because they have a fixed expiration date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No comment period is required for emergency rules and they are effective upon publication in the Register. The Register is the source for emergency rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule Review — rule-equivalent of sunset with notice & comment
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule review is the rule equivalent of the statutory sunset process and involves notice and comment similar to rule proposals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This process applies to existing, non-amended rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Searching the Register — use issue Table of Contents when citation is unknown
rubrics_metrics.description: When you lack a specific citation for a Register entry, review each issue's Table of Contents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Table of Contents is organized by type of rule and includes emergency rules, proposed rules, and adopted rules—use it to locate items when you don't have a citation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use agency websites for additional/regulatory materials (varies by agency)
rubrics_metrics.description: State agency websites often have links to an agency's rules, governing statutes, proposed rules, comments, licensing forms, and other materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Availability, format, and currency vary greatly by agency—larger, better funded agencies tend to have more information available. Check agency websites in addition to the TAC and Register.

rubrics_metrics.name: TRAIL state agency list and archives as supplemental sources
rubrics_metrics.description: The TRAIL state agency list includes links to all state agency websites, including archived versions and snapshots of sites for agencies that no longer exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use TRAIL and archival links when agency websites are missing content or when researching defunct agencies.
